xv

EDITOR'S NOTE

To commemorate the two thousand five hundredth year of the Buddha's Parinirvana, it was decided to undertake this work of editing the Pali text of the Tipitaka—the authoritative words of the Buddha—and setting it down together with a translation into our own language, out of profound reverence and devotion toward the Triple Gem. In order to carry out this task, at the encouragement of the Honourable A. Ratnayake Sirimāna, who was then the Minister of Home Affairs, the then Prime Minister of Sri Lanka, the Honourable Sir John Kotelawala, decided in the year one thousand nine hundred and fifty-five of the common era that all the texts of the Tipitaka should be edited and published, with translation into Sinhala, at state expense. In accordance with this decision, the Tipitaka Translation Board undertook this sacred task. All the learned and able monks of great renown and deep learning from every fraternity of the Sangha were brought together into this great Board.

Worthy of remembrance is the assembly gathered under the name of the Editorial Board for Tipitaka Translation of the Lanka Buddhist Mandalaya, convened by the most senior, learned and widely erudite Chief Elder then residing in this land. Among them, chosen as the foremost members of the Editorial Board, were the following Elders, who served as pioneers of this task:

Weliwitiye Sorata
Paravahera Vajiraññāna
Balangoda Ānanda Maitreya
Labugama Lankānanda
Kodagoda Ñāṇāloka

All the texts of the Tipitaka, reckoned as fifty-two volumes in all, were entrusted—each volume to its respective group of learned monks—both for the correction of the Pali text and for its careful translation into Sinhala. It has been the established custom that, once prepared by them, each volume is submitted to the Tipitaka Compilation Board, and only after further revision there is it released for printing. Today we have arrived at the final stage of this printing of the Tipitaka, a work begun some thirty-three years ago.

xvii

The exceedingly profound philosophical aspect of the Buddha's Dhamma is taught in the Abhidhamma Pitaka. Of this, the most profound and difficult-to-understand teaching is found in this Paṭṭhāna treatise. In the first part of the Paṭṭhāna treatise, as edited by the Tipitaka Council, the Sinhala exposition called "Paṭṭhāna Naya Nirūpaṇaya" was prepared by the Royal Pandit, Master of Arts, the Venerable Bellana Īṣaṇavimala Nāyaka Thera; the "Puggala Sahāga Saṅgaha" and "Puggala Saṭanāva" appearing in the third part were prepared by the Agga Mahā Pandit Ven. Balangoda Ānanda Maitreya Mahānāyaka Thera; the supplementary treatise was prepared by the Royal Pandit, Master of Arts, the Venerable Hīgoḍa Bemonanda Nāyaka Thera; and the "Paṭṭhāna Pradīpaya" found therein was prepared by the Royal Pandit Naramoṇe Buddharakkhita Thera. While all the texts of the Tipitaka have been printed together with a Sinhala translation, it is a distinctive feature that only the Paṭṭhāna treatise has been printed in the plain original language [without a full translation]. For the benefit of devout readers who do not know Pali, so that they may properly understand it, the meaning will become accessible through the aforementioned "Paṭṭhāna Naya Nirūpaṇaya," "Puggala Sahāga Saṅgaha" and "Puggala Saṭanāva," the supplementary treatise, and the "Paṭṭhāna Pradīpaya." Since the text of the Paṭṭhāna, which is analyzed by way of a hundred thousand methods, flows in one uniform manner, rendering it into the vernacular [Sinhala] was not considered essential. For one who approaches it with faith, by repeatedly practicing the method of recitation, its meaning will indeed become well clarified.

As for the Paṭṭhāna treatise, which is the largest text of the Three Baskets, it was decided from the very outset by the Tipitaka Compilation Council that it should be printed divided into three parts — the first part, the second part, and the third part. Accordingly, the first part of the Paṭṭhāna treatise was printed taking the portion of the Tika Paṭṭhāna from the Kusalattika up to the Dassanattika. The second part comprises fourteen Tikas of the Tika Paṭṭhāna, from the Dassanena-pahātabbahetuttika up to the Sanidassana-sappaṭighattika, together with twenty-two Dukas of the second Duka Paṭṭhāna, from the Hetuduka up to the Upekkhāsahagata-duka. The third part presents, together with eight Dukas of the Duka Paṭṭhāna from the Kāmāvacara-duka up to the Saraṇa-duka, the Duka-tika Paṭṭhāna, the Tika-duka Paṭṭhāna, the Tika-tika Paṭṭhāna, and the Duka-duka Paṭṭhāna.

The one who received the invitation to edit the Paṭṭhāna treatise, the 52nd text in the Buddha Jayanti Tipitaka Series of Texts, was the Agga Mahā Pandit, the Venerable Balangoda Ānanda Maitreya Mahānāyaka Swāmīndra. Though exceedingly occupied with manifold duties, yet devoted also to this very task, his Reverence [completed] the first part; [after his] passing away, [this work was carried forward by] the Royal Pandit Karahampitigoda —

xviii

With the good counsel given to the Venerable Sumanasara Nayaka Thera, he, together with the Royal Pandit Bhaigoda Bemonassa and Royal Pandit Naramane Gnanadharmakkhita Theras, carried out the proofreading of the second and third parts, and thus brought this [work] to publication.

The diligent effort made by these Theras to establish the authentic word of the Buddha, comparing it with other printed editions, is also worthy of praise.

Further, it must be stated that although the Buddhist Council intended to complete the printing within four years after editing the Tipitaka Pali text, later, since it was decided to publish it together with the Sinhala translation as well, and since none of the translated volumes done in that manner proved satisfactory, it became necessary to translate them anew, and also due to delays that occurred at certain printing presses, it was not possible to complete the printing within the originally intended time. We consider it a cause for joy to those interested in this matter that, despite the lapse of time, the aspiration of the Buddhist public who have faith in reading the entire Tipitaka Dhamma has been fulfilled by the completion of the printing of the Tipitaka volumes together with the Sinhala translation.

We commemorate with gratitude the governments of the late Sir John Kotelawala, S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike, Dudley Senanayake, Sirimavo Bandaranaike, and J.R. Jayewardene, who extended utmost support, encouragement, and patronage toward the revision and printing of the Tipitaka, a task begun in 1956 and completed in 1989. We also record with pleasure that President R. Premadasa, who served as Secretary of the Committee from the very inception of the Buddhist Council, showed faithful support from the beginning of the Tipitaka compilation effort.

The devoted interest shown with faith, reverence, and devotion by the Honourable Minister of Cultural and Religious Affairs, V.J.M. Lokubandara, in the preparation and printing of this volume, which forms the final part of the Patthana Prakarana, deserves to be remembered with gratitude. Likewise, the Honourable Secretary of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, Mr. Walter Ladduwahetti, and the Additional Secretary of the same Ministry, Mrs. Asoka Gunawardena, are also worthy of praise in this regard.

xix

The enthusiasm of Mrs. Leela Dasanayake, Deputy Director of the Literature and Publications Division of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, must also be appreciated here. Mr. S. D. Saparamadu, former civil servant, proprietor of the Kisara Press located at Dutugemunu Mawatha, Dehiwala, which printed all 29 volumes of the Buddha Jayanti Tripitaka Series, deserves our commendation for printing this volume too correctly, cleanly, beautifully, and in good time, through great effort, dedication, devotion and reverence, by expending labour, time and wealth generously, and through the diligence of his staff.

The noble religious service rendered in this country since the time of King Valagamba — namely the revision of the Tripitaka and its rendering into Sinhala — took place over a period of thirty years. With the printing of the third part of the Patthana-prakarana, that work has come to completion. Of the great elder monks who lived in this country, both in the more distant past and those who participated in this present undertaking, very few remain alive today. Therefore, we pray that through the merit of this great accumulated good deed, those venerable spiritual fathers who have passed away may attain the bliss of Nibbana. Likewise, we wish that all the distinguished and accomplished gentlemen and ladies connected with this work may attain Nibbana. May all beings attain Nibbana.

May the heroic Dispensation of the Fully Self-Enlightened One endure in this world!

Thus,

Labugama Lankananda
Mahanayaka Thera
Chairman and Chief Editor,
Tripitaka Compilation Board.

10th February, 1989
Pravachanodaya Pirivena,
Molligoda.

93. The Sensuous-Sphere Dyad (Kamavacara Duka)

Not depending on a sensuous-sphere state—

**1138 The Book of Conditional Relations (Paṭṭhāna)**

Depending on states that are both sense-sphere and non-sense-sphere — by root-condition —. Depending on one non-sense-sphere aggregate, three aggregates and mind-originated [matter arise] —. Two [kinds of matter] —. At the moment of rebirth-linking —.

Depending on a state that is both sense-sphere and non-sense-sphere, a sense-sphere state [arises] — by root-condition. Depending on non-sense-sphere matter together with the great essentials, mind-originated [matter arises] —. At rebirth-linking, depending on non-sense-sphere matter together with the great essentials, the produced [matter arises] —.

Depending on a state that is both sense-sphere and non-sense-sphere, a non-sense-sphere state [arises] — by root-condition. At rebirth-linking, depending on one non-sense-sphere aggregate and [another], three aggregates [arise], together with two [kinds of] matter —.

Depending on a state that is both sense-sphere and non-sense-sphere, states that are both sense-sphere and non-sense-sphere [arise] — by root-condition —. At rebirth-linking, depending on one non-sense-sphere aggregate and [another], three aggregates [arise], together with two [kinds of] matter —. Depending on non-sense-sphere matter together with the great essentials, the produced [matter arises]. (In brief.)

By root-condition, nine; by object-condition, seven; by predominance-condition, five; by proximity-condition, seven; by contiguity-condition, seven; by conascence-condition, nine; by mutuality-condition, [as stated]; by dependence-condition, nine; by sufficing-condition, seven; by pre-nascence-condition, two; by repetition-condition, two; by kamma-condition, nine; by resultant-condition, nine; by nutriment-condition, nine; by faculty-condition, nine; by jhāna-condition, nine; by path-condition, nine; by association-condition, seven; by dissociation-condition, nine; by presence-condition, nine; by absence-condition, seven; by disappearance-condition, seven; by non-disappearance-condition, nine.

Depending on a sense-sphere state, a sense-sphere state arises — not by root-condition. Depending on one rootless sense-sphere aggregate, three aggregates and mind-originated [matter arise] —. Two [kinds of] matter —. At rootless rebirth-linking — up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Depending on matter accompanying doubt, [the states] accompanying doubt [arise] —. Accompanying restlessness —. Delusion. By non-object-condition — finished.

Depending on a sense-sphere state, a sense-sphere state [arises] — not by predominance-condition —. Finished.

The Rebirth-linking Moment (Paṭisandhi-kkhaṇa) — Mind and Matter (Nāma-rūpa)

At the moment of rebirth-linking — the five aggregates known as mind-phenomena (nāma-dhamma) and matter-phenomena (rūpa-dhamma), that is, in the case of the fivefold-process existence (pañcavokāra-bhava): the rebirth-linking mental aggregates together with the heart-basis material form — these are what is meant.

(Similar to the domain of the roots/conditions.)

Kamma-born Matter (Kaṭattā-rūpa) —

Generally, both the sense-faculty matter and the heart-basis matter, being kamma-produced matter, are also called "kaṭattā-rūpa" (kamma-born matter).
(The twelve unwholesome consciousnesses pertaining to the past existence, the eight kinds of sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, and the five kinds of form-sphere wholesome consciousnesses — these twenty-five consciousnesses, in subsequent existences, naturally give rise to kaṭattā-rūpa [kamma-born matter].)

The Condition of Kamma (Kamma-paccaya)

The mental factor common to all states of consciousness that occurs in every mind-moment, known as "cetanā" (volition) — this very mental factor is called "kamma". The other consciousness and mental factors that occur together with this mental factor, as well as whatever is done, said, or thought through that mind, are also reckoned as kamma. Thus, the "kammic force" that serves as a condition either for the mind-and-matter phenomena arising together with itself, or for the mind-and-matter phenomena arising later owing to that same cause, is here termed the "kamma-paccaya" (condition of kamma). According to the circumstances of its occurrence, this has been shown to be of two kinds:

1. The co-nascent kamma-condition, and
2. The condition of kamma that is of different moments (asynchronous kamma-condition).
